paras: The lynching of an unnamed prisoner at Starke, Florida, took place in Bradford County some time before early October 1882, when lynchers broke open the county jail and hanged a Black man held on a charge of assaulting a young woman. The only account is a short item in the Starke Weekly Telegraph, known from a reprint in the Savannah Morning News, and a Tallahassee editorial later listed the killing among Florida crimes whose perpetrators were still unpunished.

According to the Telegraph, a man it called a "burly negro brute" had "some time ago" waylaid and "outraged" a "beautiful Northern girl" near Starke; neither he nor the young woman was named, and her race was not stated. He was arrested and, after what the paper called a thorough investigation, sent to jail "to await the due course of law."

The Telegraph wrote that feeling against the prisoner was so strong that "the Bradford county lynchers could not be constrained" from breaking open the prison doors. They hanged him "by the neck until he was too dead to skin," in the paper's phrase. The item gives no date, no number of lynchers, no time of day and no place of hanging, and does not say whether the man was killed at the jail or carried elsewhere.

No report of an inquest, arrest or prosecution appears in the coverage, and on 10 October 1882 the Weekly Floridian described the perpetrators of "the lynching referred to by the Starke Telegraph in Bradford" as still unpunished.

The Telegraph's item, which the Savannah Morning News reprinted without comment on 4 October 1882, treated the hanging lightly, closing with the remark that, "strange to say," settlers from the North and West kept "flocking to Bradford county in search of new hemes."

Answering the Volusia Enterprise Herald in a dispute over the Madison County murder, the Tallahassee Weekly Floridian listed the Bradford lynching alongside a lynching in Hillsborough and several murders as crimes elsewhere in the state whose perpetrators were unpunished. The Floridian did not describe the killing itself, and used it to argue that such crimes did not make any locality less safe to "strangers." No other newspaper account of the lynching, and none naming the victim, appears in the coverage.

reader.title: Lynching of an unnamed prisoner at Starke, Florida
bases: The Starke Weekly Telegraph, as quoted, said 'Bradford county lynchers' broke open the jail and hanged a prisoner awaiting trial, and a Tallahassee editorial called it a lynching (A1, A2).

The prisoner was hanged after 'lynchers' broke open the prison doors, out of 'indignation' over an alleged outrage (A1), and the Floridian called it a lynching (A2); the number of lynchers is not given and the only account is the Telegraph's, at second hand.
Both items rest on the Starke Weekly Telegraph's report: A1 quotes it and A2 only refers to 'the lynching referred to by the Starke Telegraph' (A1, A2).

accounts.label: Starke Weekly Telegraph (as reprinted)
accounts.gist: A Black man who outraged a Northern girl was jailed, but indignation was so strong that the Bradford County lynchers broke into the prison and hanged him; settlers kept coming to the county anyway.

accounts.label: Weekly Floridian editorial
accounts.gist: Lists the Bradford lynching, by reference to the Telegraph, among recent Florida crimes whose perpetrators were unpunished.

framing.detail: The Telegraph, quoted without comment by the Savannah Morning News, called the victim a 'burly negro brute' and said the lynchers 'could not be constrained', ending with the quip that settlers still flocked to the county.
The Weekly Floridian classed the lynching with murders whose perpetrators were 'still unpunished', but only to argue that such crimes did not make any section unsafe for 'strangers'.
